title: Meta Releases Dist-MoE to Solve AI's Dropless MoE Problem

tickers.name: Meta Platforms, Inc. Class A Common Stock

summary:
The SuperIntelligence Labs unit of Meta released a toolset called Dist-MoE to optimize the training and inference of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) AI models through open-source compute and communication kernels. Benchmarks using GB300 NVL72 hardware showed the library achieves a 1.40x speedup over Mixture-of-Kittens for ten-layer MXFP8 training across 64 GPUs. The system reached 3.09 PFLOP/s per GPU for NVFP4 inference across 16 GPUs and 1.86 PFLOP/s for MXFP8 training across 64 GPUs.

The library incorporates full CUDA graph support and dynamic activation packing across layers to prevent capacity-induced recompute. Edward Yang, a Meta engineer, stated that the software resolves a previous internal challenge in achieving "cudagraphable, dropless" MoE systems. Dist-MoE is integrated with the TorchTitan framework and supports BF16, MXFP8, and NVFP4 formats.

selectedTweets.text:
We’re sharing Dist-MoE, open-source library from Meta SuperIntelligence Labs (MSL @AIatMeta ). Dist-MoE provides fused communication and compute kernels for BF16/MXFP8 training and inference, plus NVFP4 inference.

✅ Fused communication and compute kernels
✅ Full CUDA graph support
✅ Dynamic activation packing across layers into a bounded buffer
✅ Dynamic, capacity-driven recompute
✅ Forward and backward kernels for BF16/MXFP8
✅ No shared-expert branch required

Some highlights from our GB300 NVL72 benchmarks:

• Up to 1.40× speedup over Mixture-of-Kittens (MoK) in our imbalanced, ten-layer MXFP8 training workload across 64 GPUs. Dist-MoE packed activation state across all ten layers with zero capacity-induced recompute.
• 3.09 useful PFLOP/s per GPU (3,090 TFLOP/s) for NVFP4 Mega inference across 16 GPUs.
• 1.86 useful PFLOP/s per GPU (1,856 TFLOP/s) for MXFP8 Staged training across 64 GPUs.
• 1.27 useful PFLOP/s per GPU (1,271 TFLOP/s) for BF16 training across 64 GPUs.
• Sub-linear scaling under imbalance: in NVFP4 inference across 16 GPUs, 8× the received rows on the busiest GPU required 4.82× the iteration time; about 40% lower iteration time per received row.

Full configurations, raw results, and measurement definitions are in the blog.

@levendlee and I also put together an interactive visual explainer covering token dispatch and combine, quantization, forward/backward kernels, activation packing, dynamic recompute, and memory planning.
